Introduction:

Understanding species distributions requires considering three types of ecological data:

R matrix — Environmental variables (sites × environment)
L matrix — Species abundance or presence/absence (sites × species)
Q matrix — Species functional traits (species × traits)

The fourth-corner problem asks:
      How do species traits (Q) relate to environmental gradients (R),
      as mediated by species abundances (L)?
The method tests:
Are environmental gradients associated with particular species traits?

Each test corresponds to one trait–environment pair.     
      
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(vegan)
library(ade4)

data(dune)
data(dune.env)

dune.trait <- data.frame(
  LifeForm = c("shr","shr","gr","gr","gr","forb","forb","forb","forb","forb",
               "forb","gr","gr","forb","shr","forb","forb","forb","gr","gr",
               "shr","forb","forb","gr","forb","gr","gr","gr","forb","forb"),
  LeafType = c("broad","broad","grass","grass","grass","broad","broad","broad","broad","broad",
               "broad","grass","grass","broad","broad","broad","broad","broad","grass","grass",
               "broad","broad","broad","grass","broad","grass","grass","grass","broad","broad"),
  SeedMass = c("med","med","small","small","small","small","small","small","small","small",
               "small","small","small","small","med","small","small","small","small","small",
               "med","small","small","small","small","small","small","small","small","small"),
  row.names = colnames(dune)
)

dune.trait[] <- lapply(dune.trait, factor)

```


```{}
set.seed(123)

fc <- ade4::fourthcorner(
  dune.env,
  dune,
  dune.trait,
  modeltype = 6
)

fc


```

Conclusion:

There is little evidence that the traits in dune.traits are strongly filtered by the environmental variables in dune.env.
This suggests the dune vegetation community is not strongly structured by the measured environmental gradients, or the dataset is too small / coarse to detect strong patterns.

Conceptual understanding

1. Why do we need three matrices (R, L, Q) to test trait–environment relationships?
    
    Because traits belong to species, environments belong to sites, and species occur at sites. The L matrix links sites to species, enabling indirect testing of trait–environment associations.
    
2. What ecological processes could produce correlations between traits and     environmental gradients?

    Environmental filtering
    Habitat specialization
    Competitive interactions selecting specific traits
    Stress gradients favoring particular life forms or seed sizes
    
3. Why do we use permutations in fourth-corner analysis instead of classical parametric tests?

    Trait–environment relationships violate assumptions of independence.
    Permutations generate a null model preserving ecological structure while testing for non-random associations

4. Look at the raw p-values before correction. Which trait–environment pairs appear to have the strongest associations?

    Moist.5 × SeedM.small (p = 0.013)
    
    Manag.HF × SeedM.small (p = 0.027)
    
    Moist.5 × LifeF.grass (p = 0.028)

    Manur.2 × SeedM.small (p = 0.016)

5. After Holm correction, no associations remain significant. What does this tell us about the strength of the ecological signal?

    Overall ecological signal is weak, 
    Sample size too small (20 sites), 
    Too many tests (inflating correction severity), OR
    Environmental and trait variables too simple

6. Why is the Holm correction more conservative than FDR? How would this affect interpretation?

    It strictly controls family-wise error rate (FWER).
    Holm penalizes multiple comparisons more heavily than FDR, often eliminating marginally significant findings.

7. Moisture seems to show some possible associations with traits. How might moisture regulate plant functional traits in grassland ecosystems?

    Wet soils favor fast-growing species
    Dry soils favor drought-tolerant traits (deep roots, shrubs, larger seeds)
    Seedling survival differs across gradients

8. Small-seeded species appear more common at high moisture levels (raw p-values). What ecological mechanisms might explain this?

    Wet soils allow mass germination of many small seeds
    Small seeds disperse widely and colonize disturbed wet sites
    Moisture reduces drought stress that disproportionately harms small seeds

9. How could management intensity influence plant traits (e.g., mowing, fertilizing, grazing)?

    Mowing favors fast-growing graminoids
    Fertilization favors tall, competitive species
    Grazing favors low-growing or grazing-tolerant species

10. What are the limitations of this dataset (dune)? How might they reduce power to detect trait–environment associations?

    Only 20 sites
    Trait data limited
    Species abundances sparse → reduces statistical power.

11. If you wanted to detect stronger signals, what additional data could you collect?

    Continuous trait data (SLA, height, leaf N, root structure)
    More environmental variables (pH, nutrients, disturbance history)
    More sites and replicates
    Historically repeated surveys (temporal dimension)
